documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT — ESTABLISH CARE / PREVENTIVE

28F, PhD student in biology (3rd year, works as a research assistant in a lab on campus). Moved to the area for the program. Previously used university student health for everything; no regular PCP since coming to the US in 2018. Wants someone for the long haul and liked that she can text.

ASTHMA: dx as a teenager. Calls it mild. Uses albuterol a few times a month, more in spring and with hard runs in cold air. Never hospitalized, never intubated. No night waking lately. Has never been on a daily inhaler.

KIDNEY STONES: two episodes, the first in her early twenties before immigrating and the second in 2020 here, both passed at home with pain meds, no procedures. Never had a stone analyzed that she knows of. Dad has had 'a lot' of stones.

ALLERGIES: spring and late-summer sneezing, itchy eyes; was told years ago it is dust mites and pollen. Manages without regular meds. No drug allergies.

MEDS: albuterol HFA 1-2 puffs q4-6h prn.

PMH as above. PSH none. OB: G0.
FHx: mother asthma; mother also told she had a weak cervix and her brother was born early. Father recurrent kidney stones. Maternal grandmother type 2 diabetes.
SH: Never smoked. Alcohol a drink or two a month. Runs about 5 miles most days. Lives in Hadley with her two cats. Two COVID doses this spring through the university.

ROS: negative except seasonal nasal symptoms.

EXAM: Well-appearing, thin. HEENT: TMs clear, mild pale nasal mucosa, oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no LAD, thyroid normal. Lungs clear, no wheeze, good air movement. Heart RRR, no murmur. Abd soft, NT, no CVA tenderness. Skin no rash. Ext no edema.

A/P
1. Mild persistent asthma — albuterol PRN, refilled. Reviewed technique with spacer.
2. Recurrent nephrolithiasis — two episodes. Fluids, aim for pale urine. BMP and UA today. If another stone, strain it so we can get an analysis.
3. Allergic rhinitis, pollen — symptomatic, OTC options discussed, she declines for now.
4. Health maintenance: Pap last done 2020 at student health, normal per pt, will request records. Flu shot when it arrives. CBC, BMP, lipids, UA today.

RTC 1 year or prn.

documents.author: patient
documents.body: Good morning! I took a home test this weekend and it was positive, then another one this morning, also positive. My last period started Dec 31. This was planned, we're happy but I have no idea what to do first. Do I come see you or go straight to an OB? Also is my inhaler ok to keep using?

documents.title: RE: Pregnancy test
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Congratulations! That puts you at about 4-5 weeks. I've sent a referral to obstetrics; they usually see people for the first visit around 10-12 weeks and will do the dating and first labs. Yes, keep using your albuterol when you need it. Untreated asthma is a bigger risk to the pregnancy than the inhaler. Call any time with questions.

documents.title: Obstetrics — Initial Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS & GYNECOLOGY
Initial prenatal visit — 2022-03-28
Copy to primary care physician.

28 y/o G1P0 at 12w3d by LMP 2021-12-31, EDD 2022-10-07. Planned pregnancy. Mild nausea, otherwise doing well. No vaginal bleeding, no cramping or contractions, no leakage of fluid.

She is a committed distance runner, currently about 5 miles a day at a moderate pace, and her main question today is whether she can keep that up.

PMH: mild persistent asthma (albuterol prn), recurrent kidney stones, seasonal allergies.
Meds: albuterol inhaler prn.
Allergies: dust mites, pollen. NKDA.
Family: her mother was told she had cervical incompetence and her brother was born prematurely. Mother also has asthma. Father with kidney stones; maternal grandmother with type 2 DM.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol since positive test. Graduate student.

Vitals within normal limits. General exam unremarkable. Uterus palpable just above the symphysis, size consistent with dates. FHT by Doppler 150s, regular.

Assessment / plan
— IUP at 12 weeks, uncomplicated so far.
— Family history of cervical insufficiency in her mother: we discussed that this raises her own risk somewhat. Recommended scaling back from daily 5-mile runs to shorter, lower-intensity sessions on most days, with walking, swimming or prenatal yoga as alternatives; avoid high-impact intervals. Cervical length assessment with her anatomy scan.
— Asthma: continue albuterol as needed.
— Prenatal labs sent today (results below). Rubella and other immunity labs per routine.
— RTC 4 weeks.

Prenatal labs 2022-03-29: HIV Ag/Ab nonreactive. HBsAg nonreactive. HCV Ab nonreactive. RPR nonreactive.

documents.title: Running and inhaler
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi Dr, the OB asked me to cut back on running because of my mom's history. I switched to 2 miles easy and some prenatal yoga. Pollen season is starting and I've used the inhaler maybe twice this week. Is that okay or too much?

documents.title: RE: Running and inhaler
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: That sounds very reasonable. A couple of puffs twice a week during pollen season is fine. If you start needing it most days, waking at night, or it isn't working as well, message me or come in. Rinse your face and change clothes after being outside on high pollen days, it does help.

documents.title: Obstetrics — Prenatal Visit, 24 Weeks
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS & GYNECOLOGY
Prenatal visit — 2022-06-17
cc: primary care

28 y/o G1P0 at 24w0d. Has modified her exercise as advised (shorter easy runs, prenatal yoga). Feels well apart from some tiredness. No bleeding, contractions or fluid.

Exposure history obtained today: two cats at home, and a few months ago she took in a stray that she has been feeding and whose litter box she has been scooping herself.

Vitals normal. Exam unremarkable.

Ultrasound (growth and anatomy follow-up) today: bilateral ventriculomegaly; intracranial calcifications; mild fetal ascites. Estimated fetal weight small for gestational age.

TORCH serologies:
Toxoplasma IgG — positive
Toxoplasma IgM — positive
Rubella IgG — positive (immune); Rubella IgM — negative
CMV IgG — positive; CMV IgM — negative
Parvovirus B19 IgG — positive; Parvovirus B19 IgM — negative

Assessment: serology with positive Toxoplasma IgM and IgG together with the ultrasound findings is concerning for congenital toxoplasmosis.
Plan: urgent maternal-fetal medicine consultation (scheduled 6/22) for counseling, confirmatory testing and treatment. Advised to stop handling cat litter entirely; someone else should do it, or gloves and daily changes if unavoidable. Wash hands after handling cats, avoid undercooked meat. Long discussion; she is understandably upset. Social work contact offered.

Will keep primary care informed.

documents.title: Phone Call — Checking In
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt after receiving OB note from 6/17. She had already heard the results from OB and has the MFM appointment tomorrow. Tearful but has support. Questions mostly about what the cats mean now; reviewed that OB/MFM will guide testing and treatment, and that someone else should handle the litter. Asthma ok, albuterol about twice a week. Offered visit or call any time. She will send an update after MFM.

documents.title: Maternal-Fetal Medicine Consultation
documents.author: maternal-fetal medicine
documents.body:
MATERNAL-FETAL MEDICINE — CONSULTATION
Date of service: 2022-06-22
Referring: obstetrics. Copy: primary care.

Reason: positive maternal Toxoplasma IgM/IgG with fetal ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcifications, mild ascites and SGA at 24 weeks.

History reviewed with the patient. Exposure to a newly adopted stray cat's litter in recent months. No fevers or adenopathy she recalls. Medications: albuterol prn. NKDA.

Targeted ultrasound today confirms the referring findings.

Counseling: we discussed that the ultrasound findings with maternal serology strongly suggest fetal infection. Amniocentesis for Toxoplasma PCR on amniotic fluid was offered to confirm and she elected to proceed. Procedure performed today under ultrasound guidance without complication.

Plan: amniotic fluid Toxoplasma PCR sent. If positive, treatment with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin for the remainder of the pregnancy, with CBC monitoring here. Serial ultrasound with us every 2-4 weeks. Pediatric infectious disease will be involved before delivery.

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets (50 mg) twice daily for 2 days, then 2 tablets (50 mg) once daily
Take 2 tablets (1,000 mg) three times daily

documents.title: Maternal-Fetal Medicine — Result and Treatment
documents.author: maternal-fetal medicine
documents.body:
MATERNAL-FETAL MEDICINE — FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 2022-06-30

Amniotic fluid Toxoplasma gondii PCR (collected 6/22, resulted 6/28): POSITIVE. This confirms fetal infection.

Treatment started today at 25w6d:
- Pyrimethamine 50 mg PO twice daily x 2 days, then 50 mg daily
- Sulfadiazine 1,000 mg PO three times daily
- Leucovorin (folinic acid) 10 mg PO daily
Continue until delivery. Weekly CBC with us while on pyrimethamine. Good oral hydration encouraged on sulfadiazine, particularly given her history of kidney stones.

Asthma: albuterol prn, she reports more use lately with nighttime cough; advised she contact her PCP if it persists.

Next MFM ultrasound 2 weeks. Pediatric ID consult arranged for delivery planning.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD — date of service 2022-07-06
Forwarded to primary care.

CC: wheezing, cough, SOB

HPI: 28 y/o G1 at 26w5d, followed by OB and MFM for fetal toxoplasmosis, with mild persistent asthma. Two weeks of on-and-off cough, wheeze and breathlessness that has been getting steadily worse. Worst at night and when she tries her prenatal yoga class. Using albuterol 3-4 times a week now and says it barely helps. She has been reluctant to take more medicine because of the pregnancy but is now more worried about her breathing. No fever, no chest pain. No contractions, bleeding or leakage of fluid.

Meds: albuterol HFA prn; pyrimethamine 50 mg daily, sulfadiazine 1 g TID, leucovorin 10 mg daily (MFM).
Allergies: dust mites, pollen. NKDA.
SH: never smoker, no alcohol in pregnancy. Graduate student.

Triage: RR 22, SpO2 96% RA. Afebrile.
Exam: mild increased work of breathing, speaking full sentences. Bilateral expiratory wheezes throughout. Heart regular. Gravid abdomen, nontender.

ED course: albuterol/ipratropium nebulizer x3 back to back. Prednisone 40 mg PO given. OB triage at bedside: FHT 140s, reassuring; no contractions on toco. After treatments wheeze much improved, moving air well, ambulatory without desaturation.

Impression: mild persistent asthma with acute exacerbation, uncontrolled.

Disposition: discharged. Prednisone 40 mg daily to complete 5 days (rx sent). Albuterol 2-4 puffs every 4 hours as needed for the next few days. Follow up with PCP within the week; return for worsening breathing, fever, or any obstetric concerns.

Worried the prednisone hurt the baby; reassured.

A/P: Asthma exacerbation, resolved after burst. Continue albuterol as needed. Reviewed warning signs and when to use it. Call if needing it more than a couple times a week. ED record reviewed. Next OB/MFM visits as scheduled. Message me with anything.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — date of service 2022-08-10

29 y/o G1 at 31w5d, h/o recurrent kidney stones and asthma (ED visit for exacerbation last month). Two days of fever, shaking chills and right-sided flank pain, with burning on urination and going much more often. No vomiting. Denies contractions, vaginal bleeding or leakage of fluid. On MFM treatment for fetal toxoplasmosis.

Meds: pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, leucovorin; albuterol prn. NKDA (env: dust mites, pollen).

T 38.9 C (102 F), BP 120/78, HR 110, RR 18.
Uncomfortable, flushed. Lungs clear. Right CVA tenderness. Gravid abdomen soft, no uterine tenderness. FHT reassuring.

UA: pyuria, bacteriuria, leukocyte esterase positive. Urine culture sent.

Impression: acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
Plan: IV fluids, ceftriaxone IV. Admit to antepartum service.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY — ANTEPARTUM SERVICE
Admitted 2022-08-10, discharged 2022-08-13

Diagnosis: acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy, 31-32 weeks.

Course: admitted from the ED with fever, right flank pain and urinary symptoms. Started on IV ceftriaxone. Defervesced and afebrile from 48 hours on, with marked improvement in flank pain. Urine culture: E. coli >100,000 CFU/mL, susceptible to ceftriaxone and cephalexin. Fetal monitoring reassuring throughout; no preterm contractions. Continued MFM toxoplasmosis regimen inpatient.

Discharge medications:
- Cephalexin 500 mg PO four times daily to complete 14 days of antibiotics
- Pyrimethamine 50 mg daily, sulfadiazine 1 g TID, leucovorin 10 mg daily (unchanged)
- Albuterol inhaler prn

Follow-up: OB/MFM next week. PCP follow-up after discharge. Return for fever, flank pain, contractions or bleeding.

A/P: Pyelonephritis, clinically resolved, finish cephalexin. Hydration, especially with sulfadiazine and her stone history. OB to follow cultures. Call for fever or flank pain.

documents.author: obstetrics

OBSTETRIC DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 2022-09-26, discharged 2022-09-28

29 y/o G1 now P1, admitted in spontaneous labor at 38w3d. Pregnancy complicated by fetal toxoplasmosis on maternal pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin since 25w6d, pyelonephritis at 31 weeks, and one asthma exacerbation at 26 weeks.

Spontaneous vaginal delivery 2022-09-26. Pediatric team present; infant admitted to the newborn unit for evaluation and treatment of congenital toxoplasmosis under pediatric infectious disease.

Maternal postpartum course uncomplicated. Afebrile, ambulating, voiding, pain well controlled.

Maternal medications at discharge: pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin DISCONTINUED at delivery. Continue albuterol prn.

Follow-up: postpartum visit with OB in 6 weeks. PCP follow-up as usual.

documents.title: Obstetrics & Gynecology — Postpartum Follow-up
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS & GYNECOLOGY — clinic note, date of service 2023-02-07, addendum 2023-02-09
Faxed to primary care; PCP called directly 2/9.

29 y/o P1, about 4.5 months postpartum after SVD 9/26/22, here for a follow-up visit. She reports a cough for the past 3 weeks that will not go away, drenching sweats at night, and she has lost 5 kg over the same 3 weeks without trying. Has mild persistent asthma; albuterol has not changed the cough. She came to the US from a country where TB is common, about 5 years ago.

T 38.2 C. RR 22. SpO2 97% on room air.
Thin, tired-appearing. Crackles heard at both lung fields. Breasts and abdomen unremarkable. Uterus involuted.

CBC and BMP drawn today: within normal limits.
Tuberculin skin test placed today.

ADDENDUM 2/9: TST read at 48 hours, 15 mm induration. Called PCP, who is seeing her today for chest imaging and sputum. Advised a mask around others in the meantime.

events.reason: Positive TST with cough, fever, night sweats

reports.text: PA and lateral chest. Patchy airspace opacities in both upper lobes. No cavitation. No pleural effusion. No hilar or mediastinal widening. Heart size normal. Bones intact.
reports.conclusion: Patchy bilateral upper-lobe opacities without cavitation or effusion. In the setting of a positive TST, findings are suspicious for pulmonary tuberculosis; correlate with sputum.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen at end of day in the separate room, pt and staff in N95s.

OB called earlier: TST 15 mm today at 48h. Pt has had ~3 wks of cough, mostly dry, some mornings productive of a little whitish sputum, no blood. Night sweats soaking her shirt most nights. Down 5 kg. Fevers in the evenings. No chest pain. Asthma inhaler doesn't touch it. Came to the US 2018; no known TB contact she's aware of; no prior TST or IGRA she can remember. Nobody at home sick that she knows of.

Recent OB vitals 2/7 and today's reviewed. Thin, tired. No lymphadenopathy. Lungs: crackles heard on both sides, no wheeze. Heart RRR. No hepatosplenomegaly.

CXR today (read back same day): patchy opacities both upper lobes, no cavity, no effusion.

A/P
Suspected active pulmonary TB: positive TST, symptoms, fever, weight loss and upper-lobe opacities.
- Sputum x3 for AFB smear, NAAT and culture: first tonight/tomorrow AM at home with kit, then 2 more mornings. Instructions given.
- HIV test today; baseline LFTs.
- Home isolation until cleared: no lab, no campus, masks with anyone in the home, open windows, no visitors. Letter for her department.
- Reported to the local board of health today as suspected TB; referral to the public health TB clinic for treatment and contact evaluation.
- Asthma: albuterol prn.
I'll call her with results. Long talk, she is scared, mostly about the baby; told her the health department team will walk the household through screening.

documents.title: Call — Board of Health
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Public health nurse from the board of health returned our report. They have the case and will contact pt today to arrange the TB clinic intake. Sputum kits: pt dropped off specimen #1 this morning, #2 and #3 tomorrow and Monday. CXR report and visit note faxed to the TB clinic per their request.

documents.title: HIV test result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your HIV test from yesterday is negative. Liver tests are normal, which is a useful baseline for TB medicines. Still waiting on the sputum results; I'll call you as soon as they're in.

documents.title: Phone Call — Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt with sputum results. Specimen 1 AFB smear positive 1+, NAAT positive for M. tuberculosis complex with no rifampin resistance mutation. Specimens 2 and 3 smear negative. Cultures pending (weeks). This confirms pulmonary TB. Discussed that it is curable with a 6-month course of pills and that the TB clinic will run treatment with daily observed doses. Intake already set for Thu 2/16. Continue home isolation until the clinic clears her. Board of health updated by phone. She asked about the baby; the TB clinic and pediatrics are already in touch with each other. Will check in by video in a couple of weeks.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (300 mg) by mouth daily, directly observed
Take 2 capsules (600 mg) by mouth daily on an empty stomach, directly observed
Take 2 tablets (1,000 mg) by mouth daily, directly observed
Take 2 tablets (800 mg) by mouth daily, directly observed
Take 1 tablet (25 mg) by mouth daily with isoniazid

documents.title: TB Clinic — Initial Evaluation
documents.author: public health TB clinic
documents.body:
PUBLIC HEALTH TUBERCULOSIS CLINIC — INTAKE
Date: 2023-02-16
To: referring primary care physician

Thank you for the referral. 29-year-old woman, 4.5 months postpartum, foreign-born (arrived 2018), with 4 weeks of cough, fevers, night sweats and 5 kg weight loss. TST 15 mm (2/9). CXR 2/9 bilateral upper-lobe patchy opacities without cavitation. Sputum AFB smear 1+ on specimen 1, negative x2; Xpert MTB detected, rifampin resistance not detected. HIV negative 2/9. Asthma, kidney stones. NKDA.

Exam: afebrile here today, thin; scattered crackles bilaterally. Visual acuity and color vision normal. Baseline hepatic panel normal.

Assessment: pulmonary tuberculosis, smear positive, presumed drug susceptible.

Plan (weight-based dosing):
- Isoniazid 300 mg daily
- Rifampin 600 mg daily
- Pyrazinamide 1,000 mg daily
- Ethambutol 800 mg daily
- Pyridoxine 25 mg daily
Directly observed therapy by our nurses (video DOT on weekdays once established). Monthly visit with symptom review, weight, hepatic panel; monthly vision checks while on ethambutol.
Counseled: orange discoloration of urine and tears from rifampin, no alcohol, report nausea, jaundice, abdominal pain, rash, numbness or vision changes. Rifampin interacts with many drugs; check with us before any new prescription.
Home isolation continues; we will release her once she has 3 negative smears and clinical improvement on treatment.
Contact investigation of the household and lab coworkers is under way by our team.

Cultures and susceptibility pending.

documents.title: Telehealth Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video, pt at home.

Two weeks into 4-drug TB therapy via the TB clinic, DOT by video. No fevers for about a week. Sweats much less. Cough still there but softer. Appetite starting to come back. Some queasiness if she takes the pills without food; the clinic told her to take them at bedtime with a snack, which helps. Urine orange as expected. No yellow eyes, rash, numbness or vision change. Not drinking alcohol. Asthma fine.

A/P: Pulmonary TB on RIPE + B6, tolerating. TB clinic managing monitoring; I'm getting their notes. Reminded her that rifampin interacts with many medicines, so anything new goes past the clinic. Will see in person once out of isolation.

results.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex isolated. Susceptible to isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol.

TB CLINIC — month 1 visit, 2023-03-22

Culture from 2/10 grew M. tuberculosis complex, pansusceptible (INH, RIF, PZA, EMB). Ethambutol discontinued today.

Symptoms: afebrile since late February; cough occasional; sweats resolved; appetite good. Weight up modestly from intake. DOT adherence 100%.

Sputum smears negative x3 since early March. Released from home isolation as of today; may return to campus and lab.

Hepatic panel normal. Vision unchanged.

Continue isoniazid 300, rifampin 600, pyrazinamide 1,000, pyridoxine 25 daily. Next visit one month, with 2-month sputum culture.

Two months of intensive-phase therapy completed. Asymptomatic apart from a rare cough. Hepatic panel normal.

Plan: stop pyrazinamide. Continuation phase isoniazid 300 mg + rifampin 600 mg daily with pyridoxine 25 mg for 4 more months, anticipated completion mid-August. Monthly visits continue.

documents.body:
First in-person since February. Continuation phase INH/RIF/B6, TB clinic notes through April reviewed (pansusceptible, 2-mo culture negative, PZA stopped). Feels 'like herself again.' Weight coming back. No cough most days. Back in the lab full time, writing up a chapter. Spring pollen bothering her eyes and nose; using albuterol about once a week on runs, which she's restarted at 2-3 miles.

Exam: well. Lungs clear. No icterus. Heart RRR.

A/P
1. Pulmonary TB, continuation phase. Doing well. TB clinic monitoring LFTs.
2. Mild persistent asthma: albuterol prn.
3. Allergic rhinitis: symptomatic, saline rinses; she'd like to avoid adding pills right now with the TB meds.
Physical in the fall.

documents.title: TB Clinic — Completion of Therapy
documents.author: public health TB clinic
documents.body:
PUBLIC HEALTH TB CLINIC — COMPLETION OF THERAPY
To: primary care physician

Your patient completed treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis today, 2023-08-17: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide (ethambutol for the first 5 weeks, until susceptibilities returned) followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin, all with pyridoxine. 26 weeks, every dose observed.

Course: afebrile and smear-negative by early March; 2-month culture no growth. Hepatic panels normal throughout. No adverse effects.

End-of-treatment chest x-ray today: clear, with resolution of the upper-lobe opacities.

Weight back up since intake.

All TB medications stopped. She is considered cured. No routine follow-up imaging needed. Please re-evaluate for TB if she develops cough lasting more than 3 weeks, fevers, night sweats or weight loss. She has a copy of her treatment record. Household contact evaluations are complete.

Case closed with the health department.

documents.title: Annual Preventive Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PHYSICAL

30F. What a year. Finished TB treatment 8/17, completion letter in chart: cured, CXR clear. Feels well, no cough, no sweats, weight back. Running 3-4 miles a few times a week. Fifth year of the PhD, deep in experiments. Child's care continues with pediatrics. Sleep better.

Asthma: albuterol maybe 2-3 times a month, mostly with runs in cold or high pollen. No nights. No ED visits this year.
Stones: none since joining. Drinks a big bottle of water at the lab.
Rhinitis: spring/late summer, tolerable.
No alcohol since the pregnancy; plans to keep it that way for now.

Meds: albuterol prn. Allergies: dust mites, pollen; NKDA.

PHQ-2: 1.

Exam: Well. BMI normal. HEENT normal, mild nasal mucosal pallor. Neck no LAD. Lungs clear. Heart RRR no murmur. Abd soft, NT. Skin normal. Ext no edema.

A/P
- Personal history of treated pulmonary TB: no further testing needed; future TSTs/IGRAs will stay positive and aren't useful; CXR + symptoms if ever needed.
- Mild persistent asthma: albuterol prn.
- Recurrent nephrolithiasis: quiet. Hydration.
- Allergic rhinitis due to pollen.
- HM: Pap due next year (age 30, co-test). Flu and COVID next month at nurse visit. HIV/HCV done in prenatal labs and HIV again in Feb, negative. CMP/CBC today.
RTC 1 yr.

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
reports.text: Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis, renal stone protocol. A 4 mm calculus is present at the right ureterovesical junction with mild right hydronephrosis and hydroureter proximal to it. Left kidney normal without hydronephrosis. No other urinary tract calculi. Appendix normal. Liver, spleen, pancreas and adrenal glands unremarkable on this noncontrast exam. Uterus and adnexa unremarkable. No free fluid.
reports.conclusion: 4 mm right UVJ stone with mild right hydronephrosis.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Service date 2025-02-18 — copy to PCP

Chief complaint: right flank pain.

31-year-old woman with a history of kidney stones (two prior episodes) woke around 11 pm with sudden severe pain in the right flank, now 6 hours, wrapping around to the right groin. Nauseated, has not vomited. No fever. No burning, frequency or visible blood in the urine. Does not think she could be pregnant. Also has mild persistent asthma; treated for pulmonary TB in 2023, completed.

Meds: albuterol inhaler prn. Allergies: dust mites, pollen. No drug allergies.
Never smoker, no alcohol.

Afebrile. BP 130/85, HR 95.
Writhing, cannot get comfortable, clearly in a lot of pain. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft without peritoneal signs. Right CVA tenderness.

UA: SG 1.015, pH 5.5, RBC 10-15/hpf, WBC 2-3/hpf, no bacteria, nitrite negative, no casts or crystals.
Urine hCG: negative.
CT A/P without contrast: 4 mm right UVJ stone with mild right hydronephrosis.

ED course: IV ketorolac and IV ondansetron with good relief. Tolerating PO.

Assessment: right ureterolithiasis, uncomplicated (no sign of infection, pain controlled).
Plan: discharge. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily until passage (up to 4 weeks), ibuprofen 600 mg q6h prn, ondansetron 4 mg ODT prn. Strain all urine and keep the stone. Push fluids. Follow up with PCP this week; urology if not passed in 2-4 weeks. Return for fever, uncontrolled pain or vomiting.

orders.reason: Recurrent nephrolithiasis, third episode; right UVJ stone

documents.title: Phone Call — ED Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Called after ED record came in (2/18, 4 mm R UVJ stone, mild hydro, UA without infection). Pain much better, using ibuprofen twice a day, no nausea since yesterday, no fever. On tamsulosin, a little lightheaded standing up, ok if she gets up slowly. Straining urine.

Third stone: placing urology referral so they can look at prevention. Bring the stone in when it passes and we'll send it for analysis. Call for fever, chills, vomiting or pain not controlled.

documents.title: Stone!
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Good news, I passed it yesterday afternoon and caught it in the strainer. It's tiny! No pain since. Should I keep taking the tamsulosin? And where do I bring the stone?

documents.title: RE: Stone!
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Great news! Dr says you can stop the tamsulosin now. Drop the stone off at the front desk in a clean dry container (no tissue) any time today and we'll send it to the lab for analysis. Keep the urology appointment, they'll want to talk about prevention.

documents.title: Stone analysis result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your stone was calcium oxalate, which is the most common kind. The urologist will go over prevention with you on the 26th; mostly it comes down to plenty of fluids and watching salt.

documents.title: Urology Consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 2025-03-26
Referring: primary care. Thank you for this referral.

HPI: 31F with a third stone episode. ED 2/18 with right renal colic; CT showed a 4 mm right UVJ stone with mild hydronephrosis. Passed spontaneously 2/23 on tamsulosin, captured. Two prior episodes, both passed without intervention. Asymptomatic now. Father with recurrent stones.

Meds: albuterol prn. NKDA.

Exam: well, no CVA tenderness.

Data: stone analysis calcium oxalate monohydrate. CT images reviewed: no residual stones on either side.

Impression: recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, currently stone free.

Recommendations:
- Fluids to make at least 2.5 L of urine a day; aim for at least 2.5-3 L intake, more on running days and in summer.
- Moderate sodium.
- Keep normal dietary calcium; do not cut out dairy.
- No medication at this time.
- Return or call with new symptoms. Follow up as needed.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
ED PHYSICIAN NOTE (DOS 2/5/2026) — forwarded to primary care

CC: cough and fever x 10 days

32-year-old woman with mild persistent asthma and recurrent kidney stones (ED last year for a right ureteral stone; ED in 2022 for an asthma flare). Pulmonary TB treated to completion in 2023. Ten days of dry cough, low-grade fevers and fatigue. It began with a sore throat; the last week she has had mild headaches. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no blood in sputum. No night sweats or weight loss. She lives in shared graduate housing and several of her housemates have had the same kind of illness in the past couple of weeks. She came back in mid-January from a winter-break trip to an area where malaria is present.

Meds: albuterol prn. Allergies: dust mites, pollen; NKDA. Never smoker.

T 38.1 C (100.6 F), HR 90, RR 18, BP 120/78.
Alert, not toxic. Oropharynx clear. Lungs: scattered crackles at both bases, no wheezing. Heart regular. No rash.

Rapid flu A/B negative. CBC: WBC 7.9, lymphocytes 46%. Malaria smear negative.
CXR: bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates.

Impression: atypical pneumonia, most likely Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila or Legionella given the cluster among housemates and the gradual course. Picture and timing do not suggest TB reactivation (no sweats or weight loss, interstitial not upper-lobe pattern, sick contacts), and malaria smear is negative. Outpatient treatment appropriate.

Plan: azithromycin 500 mg today then 250 mg daily x 4 days. Fluids and rest. Albuterol if wheezy. PCP follow-up within a week; return for shortness of breath, chest pain, high fever or if not improving in 48-72 hours.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

orders.reason: Follow-up of pneumonia, history of treated TB

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED 2/5 with atypical pneumonia (bilateral interstitial infiltrates, flu neg, malaria smear neg), on azithro, last dose tomorrow. ED note reviewed.

No fever since Saturday. Cough still there but less, not keeping her up. Energy maybe 70%. Headaches gone. Needed albuterol twice over the weekend for chest tightness with coughing fits, none since. No sweats, appetite fine.

Exam: Looks well. Afebrile, sat normal. A few fine crackles at the bases, no wheeze. Heart RRR.

A/P
Atypical CAP improving. Finish azithro. Cough can linger for weeks. Given her TB history, I'd like a repeat film in about 6 weeks to make sure it's cleared; ordered. Albuterol prn. Call if fever returns, breathing worsens, or sweats/weight loss.
